1. Title: SQL Injection via Dynamic Query Construction
   Category: Confirmed Vulnerability
   Severity: High
   Confidence: High
   File: N/A
   Line: 15
   Evidence: The code constructs a SQL query using string concatenation (`+`) with user input (`name`) before executing it against the database.
   Data Flow: `request.args.get("name")` (Source) → string concatenation → `db.execute(q)` (Sink)
   Why It Matters: An attacker can inject malicious SQL commands to bypass authentication, exfiltrate sensitive data, or modify/delete database records.
   Why It Was Detected: The query `q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"` lacks parameterization, allowing arbitrary SQL syntax to be injected.
   Recommended Fix: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) to separate code from data.
   Manual Verification Required: Yes — send a request with `?name=' OR '1'='1` to verify authentication bypass or data leakage.
   Vulnerable Code: `q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`
   Fixed Code: `q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"; db.execute(q, (name,))`

2. Title: Command Injection via Subprocess Shell Execution
   Category: Confirmed Vulnerability
   Severity: High
   Confidence: High
   File: N/A
   Line: 22
   Evidence: The code executes a shell command using `subprocess.run` with `shell=True` and dynamically concatenates user input (`host`) into the command string.
   Data Flow: `request.args.get("host")` (Source) → string concatenation → `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` (Sink)
   Why It Matters: This allows an attacker to execute arbitrary system commands on the server, leading to full system compromise.
   Why It Was Detected: `shell=True` combined with untrusted input passed via concatenation creates a direct command injection vector.
   Recommended Fix: Use `shell=False` and pass arguments as a list.
   Manual Verification Required: Yes — send a request with `?host=8.8.8.8; rm -rf /` to verify command execution.
   Vulnerable Code: `output = subprocess.run("ping -c 1 " + host, shell=True, capture_output=True)`
   Fixed Code: `subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False, capture_output=True)`

3. Title: Unsafe Deserialization (Pickle)
   Category: Confirmed Vulnerability
   Severity: High
   Confidence: High
   File: N/A
   Line: 28
   Evidence: The code deserializes data using `pickle.loads` on `request.data` without any validation or sanitization.
   Data Flow: `request.data` (Source) → `pickle.loads` (Sink)
   Why It Matters: Pickle is inherently unsafe for untrusted data. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code upon deserialization.
   Why It Was Detected: Direct use of `pickle.loads` on untrusted input is a well-known RCE vector.
   Recommended Fix: Avoid using pickle for data exchange. Use standard formats like JSON.
   Manual Verification Required: Yes — craft a malicious pickle payload and send it via POST to `/load`.
   Vulnerable Code: `obj = pickle.loads(request.data)`
   Fixed Code: `import json; obj = json.loads(request.data)`

4. Title: Hardcoded API Secret
   Category: Security Hardening
   Severity: Low
   Confidence: High
   File: N/A
   Line: 32
   Evidence: A secret key `ADMIN_TOKEN` is defined as a hardcoded string literal.
   Data Flow: N/A
   Why It Matters: If this token is used for authentication or API verification, committing this code to a public repository exposes the secret. It also violates the principle of least privilege and configuration management.
   Why It Was Detected: The string format (`sk-live-...`) strongly resembles a live API key (e.g., Stripe), and it is hardcoded rather than loaded from environment variables.
   Recommended Fix: Store secrets in environment variables or a secure vault.
   Manual Verification Required: Yes — verify if this token is used in any route logic.
   Vulnerable Code: `ADMIN_TOKEN = "sk-live-9f8e7d6c5b4a3f2e1d0c9b8a7f6e5d4c"`
   Fixed Code: `import os; ADMIN_TOKEN = os.environ.get("ADMIN_TOKEN")`

5. Title: Path Traversal
   Category: Potential Vulnerability
   Severity: Medium
   Confidence: Medium
   File: N/A
   Line: 38
   Evidence: The code constructs a file path by concatenating a base directory with user input (`name`) and opens it without validation or normalization.
   Data Flow: `request.args.get("name")` (Source) → concatenation → `open(path)` (Sink)
   Why It Matters: An attacker can request files outside the intended directory (e.g., `../../etc/passwd`), potentially leaking sensitive system files.
   Why It Was Detected: The path construction lacks input validation or normalization (e.g., `os.path.abspath`).
   Recommended Fix: Validate the input against an allowlist or normalize the path and check if it starts with the intended directory.
   Manual Verification Required: Yes — send a request with `?name=../../etc/passwd` to verify file access.
   Vulnerable Code: `path = "/var/data/" + request.args.get("name")`
   Fixed Code: `path = os.path.join("/var/data", request.args.get("name")); path = os.path.abspath(path); if not path.startswith("/var/data/"): abort(403)`

6. Title: Resource Leak (Global Database Connection)
   Category: Code Quality
   Severity: Low
   Confidence: High
   File: N/A
   Line: 14
   Evidence: The database connection `db` is established globally but never closed explicitly.
   Data Flow: N/A
   Why It Matters: The connection remains open until the application process terminates, potentially exhausting database connections or causing resource locks.
   Why It Was Detected: The connection is created outside of a context manager and has no explicit close statement.
   Recommended Fix: Use a context manager (`with sqlite3.connect(...)`) or ensure the connection is closed on application exit.
   Vulnerable Code: `db = sqlite3.connect("app.db")`
   Fixed Code: `db = sqlite3.connect("app.db"); # Ensure connection is closed on exit or use a context manager`
